profiles.meeting_scenario: At a university-affiliated pulmonary clinic, a pediatric pulmonologist and a clinical pharmacy specialist are holding a 10-turn brainstorming meeting to generate ideas for a grand rounds session titled 'Asthma therapeutics: past, present, and future.' The session is intended to be clinically useful while also highlighting how asthma care has shifted from broad controller therapy to phenotype- and endotype-informed biologics. Their agenda is to brainstorm the session structure, candidate patient examples, and future-therapy angles that will make the talk feel practical and forward-looking. The expected outcome is a short list of promising content directions and an informal division of follow-up tasks for building the presentation.

members.name: Dr. Maya Rios
members.expertise: Severe pediatric asthma, biologic eligibility assessment, airway disease phenotyping
members.background: Dr. Rios leads the severe asthma program at a children's hospital and regularly presents clinically oriented teaching sessions for fellows and community pediatricians.
members.private_state: She wants the talk to feel immediately actionable for frontline clinicians and to showcase the severe-asthma referral pathway her program has built, without making the session look like a narrow subspecialty lecture.
hidden_assumptions: When a talk is described as 'practical,' it should center on decisions a general pediatrician can make at the point of referral rather than detailed payer or infusion logistics.
A 'severe asthma' patient example naturally means a child whose disease remains uncontrolled despite optimized high-dose inhaled therapy and adherence review.
If they mention a 'future therapy' section, it can reasonably include near-clinic innovations such as expanded biologic positioning and remission-oriented care, not only drugs still in phase trials.
A 'case vignette' for teaching usually refers to one longitudinal anchor patient revisited across the talk rather than several short snapshots.

members.name: Dr. Evan Patel
members.role: Clinical Pharmacy Specialist in Allergy and Pulmonology
members.expertise: Asthma pharmacotherapy, biologic access workflows, formulary strategy, medication education
members.background: Dr. Patel supports severe asthma clinics across the health system, manages biologic education pathways, and frequently teaches clinicians about medication selection, administration, and coverage barriers.
members.private_state: He wants the session to highlight real-world implementation issues around newer therapies and to make clear that exciting treatment advances still depend on access, administration, and step-therapy constraints.
hidden_assumptions: When a talk is called 'practical,' it should include the real-world medication workflow clinicians struggle with after choosing a therapy, especially authorization, administration site, and steroid-sparing logistics.

A 'severe asthma' teaching case can appropriately include patients escalated to biologics because of recurrent exacerbations and steroid burden even if inhaler technique and adherence were not the dramatic teaching focus.

A 'future therapy' segment should mainly mean agents or modalities beyond current routine use, such as upstream epithelial targets, longer-acting formulations, or non-antibody platforms in development.
A 'case vignette' in educational sessions often means a set of two or three concise patient snapshots illustrating different mechanisms or access issues.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as a practical talk
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree the session should be 'practical' for the audience.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means practical clinical reasoning at the bedside: recognizing phenotype clues, identifying when standard therapy is failing, and knowing when to refer for biologic evaluation.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means practical implementation after treatment selection: navigating prior authorization, choosing administration setting, counseling on injection logistics, and handling steroid tapering realities.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In medical education planning, 'practical' is universally positive and usually left undefined; both interpretations sound compatible enough that neither participant feels a need to unpack the term.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to build around a 'severe asthma case.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the case must satisfy a specialist-style threshold: persistent uncontrolled disease despite confirmed adherence, proper inhaler technique, and optimized high-dose ICS-LABA before biologics enter the picture.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes a case with frequent exacerbations, repeated oral corticosteroid bursts, and eventual biologic consideration is sufficient even if optimization steps are compressed because the educational point is treatment escalation in the real world.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both routinely use the same label in clinic and teaching, and the distinction concerns evidentiary standards behind the label rather than the overt management pathway, so the gap stays invisible during a brainstorming conversation.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say they want to end with 'future therapies.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes this includes near-future clinical practice shifts built from current biologics and remission concepts, such as earlier phenotype-guided use, de-escalation questions, and broader pediatric application.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes this means therapies not yet part of standard daily practice, such as anti-alarmin pipeline agents beyond currently approved use, depot approaches, inhaled biologic delivery concepts, or gene/RNA-based strategies.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'future therapies' naturally spans both adjacent clinical evolution and true pipeline innovation, so each hears the phrase as comfortably broad enough to include their own intended boundary.

misalignment_points.topic: How many case vignettes they are building
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to 'start with a case vignette and come back to it later.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 pictures one longitudinal anchor patient whose history, escalation, and response are threaded through the entire talk to maintain narrative coherence.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 pictures an opening vignette followed by a return to a small cluster of brief contrasting cases, such as eosinophilic asthma, allergic asthma, and steroid-dependent asthma, each illustrating a different therapeutic angle.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Educational presenters often use the singular 'case vignette' loosely even when they mean a recurring case framework or a short series of cases, so the procedural difference hides beneath familiar presentation jargon.

turns.inner_thought: I want this to land with general pediatricians and fellows, not just severe-asthma specialists. If we call it practical, it should help them recognize when usual management is failing, what clues matter, and when to send a child into a referral pathway like ours. The title also gives us room to show the arc from broad controller therapy to phenotype-guided care, and by future therapies I can include where current biologics are heading over the next few years.

A severe asthma case would give us a clean way to walk through escalation without getting lost in history slides, and a case vignette can easily be a framework we revisit with a few contrasting examples later.
